description: Chain level joint translation. A chain is translated as one unit: its members are merged into a single source text, that text is translated whole, and the translation is cut back into one piece per member. Everything the two halves of that round trip need is declared here. output_token_budget and output_token_ratio bound how large a chain may be sent as one unit: the engine is called with a fixed output ceiling, and a request whose answer would reach it comes back truncated rather than refused, which no conservation check downstream can undo. The expected answer is estimated as the merged source token count times output_token_ratio -- measured at about 0.9 for a display line and 1.2 for running text on an English to Chinese pair, so the shipped coefficient carries a safety factor -- and a chain whose estimate exceeds output_token_budget is handed back to the per paragraph path whole, which is the same escape hatch every other unmergeable chain takes. The budget sits below the engine's own ceiling to leave room for the JSON envelope the answer is wrapped in. join says how two consecutive members are put back together, and records the separator it used so the merge can be read back. profiles say what a sentence end looks like in the target language and where a cut may legally land in it; the profile is chosen by the target language tag, longest declared prefix first, falling back to the default. strategies say which redistribution a chain is cut by, read from the endpoint pair class the chain was built under, never from a page type or a publication. A body chain is cut on sentence boundaries and falls back to a proportional cut only for the members no boundary is left for; a display line chain has no sentence structure to cut on and is proportional throughout. Every cut is a position in the translated string and nothing but the one page break hyphen is ever added or removed, so the pieces always join back to exactly the translation that came in. Punctuation is written as JSON unicode escapes to keep this file ASCII. A display line chain is cut by share, and a share taken from the source is the wrong quantity to cut a translation by whenever the two languages do not spend their characters at the same rate. The source break falls at an English word boundary, and there is no reason for the character at the same fraction of a Chinese translation to be a word boundary at all -- still less the boundary the source broke at. So the cut is placed by a cascade of three, each level falling softly back to the next. cut_align_switch names the run attribute the first level is read from; with it down the cascade starts at the last level, which is the placement this file described before the cascade existed. At the first level each member of the chain is translated once on its own, and the length of that answer -- never its text, which no chain output is ever built from -- gives the share the cut is placed by, so the cut lands where the translation of the first member would have ended. At the second level the estimate is moved to the nearest position within cut_snap_radius characters that follows a punctuation mark or one of the profile's cut_boundary_markers, earlier position winning a tie; a profile declaring no markers and finding no punctuation leaves the estimate where it is, which is how a language whose break rule already snaps to word boundaries takes no second placement. At the third level the cut is placed by the source share exactly as before. Two failure modes are known and neither is repaired here. Where the joint translation reorders across the boundary there is no aligned cut to find, and the cascade degrades to share plus snap with the damage bounded by the radius. And where a member's own translation differs in length from the same member's stretch of the joint translation -- context changes wording, and one request has context the other has not -- the estimate is off by that difference, which is why the radius exists and why it is small.

join.description: How consecutive members are merged. A member whose last character is a trailing hyphen is a word the page break cut in half, so the hyphen is dropped and the halves close up; the hyphen is kept when it stands alone as a word, which is what the preceding character being a space tells us. Two members that meet where neither side is written with interword spaces close up as well: spaceless_script_ranges lists the code point ranges, low..high in hexadecimal, whose scripts set no space between words. Everything else takes the default separator. Nothing else is added to or removed from a member.

profiles.description: One sentence model per target script. terminators end a sentence wherever they stand. space_gated_terminators end one only when whitespace or the end of the text follows, which is what keeps a decimal point, a version number and an in-word full stop from ending a sentence; the two lists together must not be empty. closers are the marks stripped after a terminator before the gate is read, so a quoted sentence still ends where the quotation does. A run of terminators is one boundary and the last character of the run decides whether the gate applies. non_terminal_prefixes are the abbreviations that carry a terminator and a space and still do not end a sentence; the table is read before the gate, so a boundary whose text ends in one of them is dropped whatever the gate would have said. A prefix matches only where the character in front of it is not a letter or a digit, so a longer word ending in the same letters is not mistaken for it. sentence_min_chars is the shortest sentence a boundary may close, counted in non-space characters: below it the boundary is dropped and the text carries on into the next sentence, which is what absorbs single letter initials. It is bounded by the range the flat sentence_min_chars declares. break_rule says where a proportional cut may land: word_boundary only after whitespace, any_char anywhere a combining sequence is not broken. language_prefixes match the target language tag, longest first; a prefix may be declared by one profile only.

strategies.description: Which redistribution a chain is cut by, keyed by the endpoint pair class the chain was built under in chain_detection.json. capacity places each cut where the member's own box stops holding text, measured by the line grid below, and falls back to sentence_greedy where the caller could measure no box; it is what a broken running paragraph takes, because its continuation should resume where the first box ran out of room rather than where a sentence happened to end, and that is true of a paragraph broken by a column edge and one broken by a page edge alike. sentence_greedy assigns whole sentences to members by their share of the source and cuts proportionally only where no sentence boundary is left, which it reports as a proportional fallback. proportional cuts by share throughout and claims no sentence structure. A pair class not named here takes the default.

capacity.description: The line grid a member's box is measured by, to estimate how many characters of the target language it holds. The typesetting stage's own packer cannot be called for this: it is a method of the stage, it needs the mapped font and a list of typesetting units built from laid out characters, and at the moment a chain is cut the translation has no characters yet -- so the capacity is arithmetic over the box instead, and the two numbers it needs are declared here rather than guessed at each site. line_skip_<script> is the multiple of the font size the stage advances between baselines, pinned to the value the stage itself uses. advance_ratio_<script> is the mean character advance as a multiple of the font size, measured over the body paragraphs of the frozen b11.6 runs: 1.00 for a Chinese target across three samples, and 0.473 for an English one with a tenth to ninetieth percentile spread of 0.464..0.492. Which pair a target language takes is decided by cjk_target_prefixes, by the same longest declared prefix match the indent policy resolves a language tag with. The estimate is deliberately coarse: a cut a few characters off is corrected by the break rule and the retreat that follow it, and a cut badly off is caught by the stage's own scale search the way any overfull box is.

line_head_forbidden_punctuation_descript: The marks a line may not open with, which a capacity cut pulls its continuation back off. This is the typesetting stage's own class, declared here rather than imported from it: chain_backfill is pure -- strings in, strings out, no intermediate language and no pipeline -- and importing the stage would invert that. A gate pins this list byte-equal to the stage's LINE_HEAD_FORBIDDEN_PUNCTUATION, so the two cannot drift apart; the equality is checked rather than assumed, which an import could not have given.
